Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 98, verses 1–8 (part 1 of 2):

It is Madani according to the majority of scholars, though it has been said to be Makki.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The surah *Lam yakun* was revealed in Medina."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Aisha, who said: "The surah *Lam yakun* was revealed in Mecca."

Abu Nu'aym transmitted in *al-Ma'rifa* from Isma'il ibn Abi Hakim al-Muzani, who said: Fadl told me: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Allah listens to the recitation of ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾, and says: 'Rejoice, My servant, by My might and My majesty, I will surely grant you in Paradise until you are content.'" Ibn Kathir said: "This is a very strange hadith."

Abu Musa al-Madini transmitted it from Matar al-Muzani, or al-Madani, in similar wording.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: 'Allah has commanded me to recite to you ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾.' He said: 'Did He name me to you?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he wept."

Ahmad, Ibn Qani' in *Mu'jam al-Sahaba*, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hayya al-Badri, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾ to its end, Jibril said: 'O Messenger of Allah, your Lord commands you to recite it to Ubayy.' The Prophet ﷺ said to Ubayy: 'Jibril has commanded me to recite this surah to you.' Ubayy said: 'And was I mentioned there, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he wept."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

By ﴿those who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ is meant the Jews and the Christians, and by "the polytheists" is meant the polytheists of the Arabs, who were idol-worshippers. *Munfakkin* is the predicate of *kana* (the verb "to be"). It is said: "I unfastened the thing and it became unfastened," meaning it separated. The meaning is that they were not departing from their disbelief nor ceasing from it, ﴿until there came to them the clear proof﴾. It has also been said that *infikak* means cessation and reaching an end, that is: they would not reach the end of their lifespans and die until there came to them the clear proof. It has also been said that *munfakkin* means "leaving" (ceasing): that is, their term would not end until there came to them the clear proof. It is said: "So-and-so did not cease (*ma infakka*) standing," meaning he did not stop standing. The root of *fakk* is opening, and from it comes *fakk al-khalkhal* (unfastening the anklet).

It has also been said that *munfakkin* means "departing": that is, they would not depart or leave this world until there came to them the clear proof.

Ibn Kaysan said: The meaning is that the People of the Book were not abandoning the description of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent. But when he was sent, they envied him and denied him. This is like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 89]. According to this, His saying "and the polytheists" means that they did not speak ill of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent, for they used to call him "the Trustworthy." But when he was sent, they turned hostile to him and spoke ill of him.

It has been said: *munfakkin* means "perishing," from their saying: "his spine became unfastened," meaning it separated and did not rejoin, so he perished. The meaning is: they were not punished or destroyed except after the proof had been established against them.

It has been said that the polytheists are the People of the Book, so that it is a description of them, because they said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and "Uzayr is the son of Allah."

al-Wahidi said: The meaning of the verse is God Most High informing about the disbelievers that they would not cease from their disbelief and their association of others with Allah until Muhammad ﷺ came to them with the Qur'an, which made clear to them their error and their ignorance, and called them to faith. This is an explanation of the blessing and of being rescued by him from ignorance and error. The verse refers to those from both groups who believed.

He said: This verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in its structure and its exegesis. Great scholars have stumbled over it, and have taken in its interpretation paths that do not lead them to the correct understanding.

The correct view is what I have informed you of. So praise Allah, who has brought you its explanation without ambiguity or difficulty.

He said: That the clear proof is Muhammad ﷺ is shown by the fact that it (the verse) explained it and put it in apposition (*badal*, substitute) to it, saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah reciting purified scriptures﴾, meaning what the scriptures contain of writings in them, which is the Qur'an. This is also shown by the fact that he used to recite from memory, not from a book. End of his words.

It has also been said that the verse is a report of what the People of the Book and the polytheists used to say: that they would not depart from their religion until the promised Prophet was sent. But when he was sent, they split apart, as Allah related about them in this surah.

The clear proof, according to what the majority have said, is Muhammad ﷺ, because he himself is a clear proof and an argument. For this reason Allah named him "a radiant lamp."

Allah, glory be to Him, explained this general "clear proof" by His saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾, so the matter became manifest and it was made clear that he is what is meant by "the clear proof."

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: The clear proof is the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]. Abu Muslim said: What is meant by "the clear proof" is the messengers in general, and the meaning is: until there come to them messengers from Allah, who are the angels, reciting to them purified scriptures. The first view is more preferable.

The majority read ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾. Ibn Mas'ud read: "The polytheists and the People of the Book." Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a reading given in the manner of explanation, not in the manner of recitation.

al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i read *wal-mushrikun* (and the polytheists) with the *raf'* (nominative) case, in coordination with the relative pronoun.

Ubayy read: ﴿So those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not...﴾ (*fa-ma kana*).

The majority read ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾ with *rasulun* in the nominative, as a *badal kull min kull* (a full substitute for the whole, for emphasis), or as a *badal ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion).

al-Zajjaj said: *Rasulun* is in the nominative as a substitute for "the clear proof."

al-Farra' said: It is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject: that is, "it is a messenger" or "he is a messenger."

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *rasulan* in the accusative, as a *qat'* (separation). The phrase *min Allah* is attached to an omitted element which is a description of *rasul*, meaning: "coming from Allah." It is also permissible for it to be attached to *rasul* itself. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *suhuf* (scriptures), with the implied meaning: "reciting purified scriptures sent down from Allah." His saying ﴿reciting purified scriptures﴾ may be another description of *rasul*, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the preceding prepositional phrase.

The meaning of *yatlu* is "recites." It is said: "talā yatlū tilāwa." *Suhuf* is the plural of *sahifa*, which is the container of what is written. The meaning of *muṭahhara* (purified) is that they are free of falsehood and error.

Qatada said: "Purified" means free of falsehood. It has been said: "purified" means free of lies, doubts, and disbelief. The meaning is one. The meaning is that he recites what the scriptures contain of writings in them, because he ﷺ used to recite from memory, not from a book, as has already been mentioned.

His saying ﴿in them are upright books﴾ is a description of *suhuf*, or a circumstantial clause from its pronoun. What is meant is the verses and the rulings written in them. *Qayyima* means straight, upright, correct, firm, from the Arab saying: "the thing stood" when it became straight and sound.

Sahib al-Nazm said: *Kutub* here means a ruling, like His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers shall surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], meaning He ruled. And the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the story of the labourer: "I will surely judge between you two by the Book of Allah," and then he ruled for stoning, though stoning is not in the Book of Allah. So the meaning is: "I will surely judge between you two by the ruling of Allah." By this is answered what has been said: that *suhuf* are the books, so how could He say ﴿purified scriptures, in them are books﴾?

al-Hasan said: By the purified scriptures is meant those that are in heaven, that is, in the Preserved Tablet, as in His saying: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21–22].

﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear proof had come to them.﴾ This sentence is a new independent sentence, to rebuke and reprimand the People of the Book, and to explain that what is attributed to them of not departing was not due to confusion of the matter, but was after the truth had become clear and the right course had become manifest.

The exegetes said: The People of the Book were continuously united until Allah sent Muhammad. But when he was sent, they split over his matter and differed. Some of them believed in him and others disbelieved.

He singled out the People of the Book, although others were like them in dividing after the coming of the clear proof, because they were people of knowledge. When they divided, those who had no scripture were included in this description. The exception in His saying ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ is a "restricted" exception from the most general of times: that is, they did not divide at any time except after the clear proof had come to them, namely the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with the glorious law and the white path.

It has been said: "The clear proof" is the explanation that is in their books, that he is a sent prophet, as in His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ except after the knowledge had come to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: From the beginning of the surah to His saying ﴿upright books﴾, its ruling concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who believed.

His saying ﴿And they did not divide...﴾ and so on concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who did not believe after the proofs had been established.

The clause ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause, serving to rebuke and reprimand them for what they did of dividing after the clear proof had come. That is: and the situation is that they were not commanded in their books except for the purpose that they should worship Allah and make Him one, while ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, that is, making their religion pure for Him, glory be to Him, or making themselves pure for Him in religion. It has been said that the *lam* in *liya'budu* (that they might worship) has the meaning of *an* (that): that is, they were not commanded except that they should worship, as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], meaning that He make clear; and ﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 8], meaning that they extinguish.

The majority read *mukhlisin* with a kasra on the *lam*. Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it.

This verse is among the proofs indicating the obligation of intention in acts of worship, because sincerity is an act of the heart. The accusative of *hunafa'* is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *mukhlisin*, so it is of the type of overlapping (*tadakhul*). It is also permissible that it be from the subject of *ya'budu*, and the meaning is: inclining away from all religions towards the religion of Islam.

The people of the language said: The origin of it is that one turns (*yahnif*) towards the religion of Islam, that is, inclines towards it. ﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, that is, perform the prayers at their times and give the zakat at its due time. The prayer and the zakat are singled out because they are among the greatest pillars of the religion.

It has been said: If by the prayer and the zakat is meant what is in the law of the People of the Book of prayer and zakat, then the matter is clear. If what is meant is what is in our law, then the meaning of His commanding them with both in the two scriptures is that He commanded them to follow our law, and both are among what was commanded in them.

﴿And that is the upright religion﴾, that is, that mentioned: worshipping Allah and making it sincere, and establishing the prayer and zakat, ﴿is the upright religion﴾, that is, the religion of the straight community.

al-Zajjaj said: That is the religion of the straight community, so *al-qayyima* is an adjective of an omitted noun.

al-Khalil said: *Al-qayyima* is the plural of *al-qayyim*, and *al-qayyim* means the upright one.

al-Farra' said: He attributed the religion to *al-qayyima*, which is its description, because the two words differ. He also said: It is an attribution of a thing to itself, and the *ha'* (feminine marker) entered for praise and emphasis.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, clarified the condition of the two groups in the Hereafter after clarifying their condition in this world, and said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell﴾. The relative pronoun is the subject of *inna*, *al-mushrikin* is coordinated with it, and its predicate is ﴿in the fire of Hell﴾, and ﴿abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun implied in the predicate. It is also permissible that His saying *wal-mushrikin* be in the genitive case, coordinated with *ahl al-kitab*. The meaning of their being in the fire of Hell is that they will go to it on the Day of Resurrection. The indication in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those previously mentioned among the People of the Book and the polytheists, who are characterised by being in the fire of Hell and abiding in it, ﴿they are the worst of creation﴾, that is, of the creatures. It is said: *bara'a* means "he created," *al-bari'* is the Creator, and *al-bariyya* is the creation.

The majority read *al-bariyya* without a hamza in both places. Nafi' and Ibn Dhakwan read it with a hamza in both places.

al-Farra' said: If you take *al-bariyya* from *al-bara'* (dust), the angels do not enter under this word. If you take it from *bariytu al-qalam* (I shaped the pen, meaning I made it), then they enter.

Some have said that the hamza is the original form, since one says "Allah bara'a al-khalq bi-l-hamz," meaning He originated and invented the creation. From this is His saying: ﴿before We bring it into being﴾ [al-Hadid: 22]. But the hamza was lightened, and its lightening was made obligatory according to the majority of the Arabs.

Then He explained the state of the other group, saying: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, meaning those who combined faith with righteous action, those are the ones described by this: ﴿they are the best of creation﴾. He said: What is meant is that those are the worst of creation in his time (ﷺ), and it is not far-fetched that among the disbelieving nations there may be someone worse than them. And these are the best of creation in his time (ﷺ), and it is not far-fetched that among the believers of earlier nations there may be someone better than them.

﴿Their reward with their Lord﴾, meaning their recompense with their Creator in return for what proceeded from them of faith and righteous action: ﴿Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow﴾. What is meant by "Gardens of Eden" is the middlemost and best of the gardens. It is said: "adana bi-l-makan ya'dunu adnan," meaning he resided. The "ma'din" (source/origin) of a thing is its center and its place of settlement. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And if they are compared to his knowledge, they are compared to a superior one who has settled (qad 'adan)."

We have mentioned in more than one place that if by the gardens are meant the thick-leaved trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is evident; and if what is meant is the totality of the ground's floor and the trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is by reference to its apparent part, which is the trees. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾: they will not leave them nor depart from them, but rather they will remain perpetually in its bliss, continuing in its pleasures. ﴿Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.﴾ The sentence is resumed to explain what Allah has bestowed upon them beyond mere recompense, namely His good pleasure with them, in that they obeyed His command and accepted His laws; and their pleasure with Him, in that they attained of desires what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

It is also permissible that the sentence be a second predicate, or that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause with "qad" understood. ﴿That is for him who fears his Lord﴾: that is, that recompense and good pleasure are for the one in whom the fear of Allah the Exalted arose in this world and who refrained from His disobedience because of that fear which had come to him, not mere fear accompanied by persistent immersion in acts of disobedience to Allah the Exalted, for that is not true fear.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying "munfakkin" (separate), that he said: "barihin" (departing).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you marvel at the rank of the angels with Allah? By Him in whose hand is my soul, the rank of the believing servant with Allah on the Day of Resurrection is greater than the rank of an angel. Recite, if you wish: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'isha, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, who is the most noble of creation before Allah? He said: O 'A'isha, do you not recite ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾?"

Ibn 'Asakir related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) when 'Ali came. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: By Him in whose hand is my soul, this man and his partisans are the victorious on the Day of Resurrection. And the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾. So whenever he came, the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) would say: The best of creation has come."

Ibn 'Adi and Ibn 'Asakir related from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "'Ali is the best of creation."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to 'Ali: It is you and your partisans on the Day of Resurrection, well-pleased and well-pleasing."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the best of creation? They said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah. He said: A man who holds the bridle of his horse in the way of Allah, whenever an alarm sounds he mounts it. Shall I not inform you of the worst of creation? They said: Yes. (p-1645) He said: The one who asks by Allah but does not give by Him."

Ahmad said: Ishaq ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Abu Ma'shar narrated to us, from Abu Wahb, the client of Abu Hurayra, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.

The Prophet ﷺ said to Ubayy: 'Jibril has commanded me to recite this surah to you.' Ubayy said: 'And was I mentioned there, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he wept."

It has also been said that *infikak* means cessation and reaching an end, that is: they would not reach the end of their lifespans and die until there came to them the clear proof. It has also been said that *munfakkin* means "leaving" (ceasing): that is, their term would not end until there came to them the clear proof. It is said: "So-and-so did not cease (*ma infakka*) standing," meaning he did not stop standing. The root of *fakk* is opening, and from it comes *fakk al-khalkhal* (unfastening the anklet).

It has also been said that *munfakkin* means "departing": that is, they would not depart or leave this world until there came to them the clear proof.

Ibn Kaysan said: The meaning is that the People of the Book were not abandoning the description of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent. But when he was sent, they envied him and denied him. This is like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 89]. According to this, His saying "and the polytheists" means that they did not speak ill of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent, for they used to call him "the Trustworthy." But when he was sent, they turned hostile to him and spoke ill of him.

It has been said: *munfakkin* means "perishing," from their saying: "his spine became unfastened," meaning it separated and did not rejoin, so he perished. The meaning is: they were not punished or destroyed except after the proof had been established against them.

It has been said that the polytheists are the People of the Book, so that it is a description of them, because they said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and "Uzayr is the son of Allah."

al-Wahidi said: The meaning of the verse is God Most High informing about the disbelievers that they would not cease from their disbelief and their association of others with Allah until Muhammad ﷺ came to them with the Qur'an, which made clear to them their error and their ignorance, and called them to faith. This is an explanation of the blessing and of being rescued by him from ignorance and error. The verse refers to those from both groups who believed.

He said: This verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in its structure and its exegesis. Great scholars have stumbled over it, and have taken in its interpretation paths that do not lead them to the correct understanding.

The correct view is what I have informed you of. So praise Allah, who has brought you its explanation without ambiguity or difficulty.

He said: That the clear proof is Muhammad ﷺ is shown by the fact that it (the verse) explained it and put it in apposition (*badal*, substitute) to it, saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah reciting purified scriptures﴾, meaning what the scriptures contain of writings in them, which is the Qur'an. This is also shown by the fact that he used to recite from memory, not from a book. End of his words.

It has also been said that the verse is a report of what the People of the Book and the polytheists used to say: that they would not depart from their religion until the promised Prophet was sent. But when he was sent, they split apart, as Allah related about them in this surah.

The clear proof, according to what the majority have said, is Muhammad ﷺ, because he himself is a clear proof and an argument. For this reason Allah named him "a radiant lamp."

Allah, glory be to Him, explained this general "clear proof" by His saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾, so the matter became manifest and it was made clear that he is what is meant by "the clear proof."

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: The clear proof is the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]. Abu Muslim said: What is meant by "the clear proof" is the messengers in general, and the meaning is: until there come to them messengers from Allah, who are the angels, reciting to them purified scriptures. The first view is more preferable.

The majority read ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾. Ibn Mas'ud read: "The polytheists and the People of the Book." Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a reading given in the manner of explanation, not in the manner of recitation.

al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i read *wal-mushrikun* (and the polytheists) with the *raf'* (nominative) case, in coordination with the relative pronoun.

Ubayy read: ﴿So those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not...﴾ (*fa-ma kana*).

The majority read ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾ with *rasulun* in the nominative, as a *badal kull min kull* (a full substitute for the whole, for emphasis), or as a *badal ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion).

al-Zajjaj said: *Rasulun* is in the nominative as a substitute for "the clear proof."

al-Farra' said: It is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject: that is, "it is a messenger" or "he is a messenger."

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *rasulan* in the accusative, as a *qat'* (separation). The phrase *min Allah* is attached to an omitted element which is a description of *rasul*, meaning: "coming from Allah." It is also permissible for it to be attached to *rasul* itself. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *suhuf* (scriptures), with the implied meaning: "reciting purified scriptures sent down from Allah." His saying ﴿reciting purified scriptures﴾ may be another description of *rasul*, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the preceding prepositional phrase.

The meaning of *yatlu* is "recites." It is said: "talā yatlū tilāwa." *Suhuf* is the plural of *sahifa*, which is the container of what is written. The meaning of *muṭahhara* (purified) is that they are free of falsehood and error.

Qatada said: "Purified" means free of falsehood. It has been said: "purified" means free of lies, doubts, and disbelief. The meaning is one. The meaning is that he recites what the scriptures contain of writings in them, because he ﷺ used to recite from memory, not from a book, as has already been mentioned.

His saying ﴿in them are upright books﴾ is a description of *suhuf*, or a circumstantial clause from its pronoun. What is meant is the verses and the rulings written in them. *Qayyima* means straight, upright, correct, firm, from the Arab saying: "the thing stood" when it became straight and sound.

Sahib al-Nazm said: *Kutub* here means a ruling, like His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers shall surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], meaning He ruled. And the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the story of the labourer: "I will surely judge between you two by the Book of Allah," and then he ruled for stoning, though stoning is not in the Book of Allah. So the meaning is: "I will surely judge between you two by the ruling of Allah." By this is answered what has been said: that *suhuf* are the books, so how could He say ﴿purified scriptures, in them are books﴾?

al-Hasan said: By the purified scriptures is meant those that are in heaven, that is, in the Preserved Tablet, as in His saying: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21–22].

﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear proof had come to them.﴾ This sentence is a new independent sentence, to rebuke and reprimand the People of the Book, and to explain that what is attributed to them of not departing was not due to confusion of the matter, but was after the truth had become clear and the right course had become manifest.

The exegetes said: The People of the Book were continuously united until Allah sent Muhammad. But when he was sent, they split over his matter and differed. Some of them believed in him and others disbelieved.

He singled out the People of the Book, although others were like them in dividing after the coming of the clear proof, because they were people of knowledge. When they divided, those who had no scripture were included in this description. The exception in His saying ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ is a "restricted" exception from the most general of times: that is, they did not divide at any time except after the clear proof had come to them, namely the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with the glorious law and the white path.

It has been said: "The clear proof" is the explanation that is in their books, that he is a sent prophet, as in His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ except after the knowledge had come to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: From the beginning of the surah to His saying ﴿upright books﴾, its ruling concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who believed.

His saying ﴿And they did not divide...﴾ and so on concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who did not believe after the proofs had been established.

The clause ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause, serving to rebuke and reprimand them for what they did of dividing after the clear proof had come. That is: and the situation is that they were not commanded in their books except for the purpose that they should worship Allah and make Him one, while ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, that is, making their religion pure for Him, glory be to Him, or making themselves pure for Him in religion. It has been said that the *lam* in *liya'budu* (that they might worship) has the meaning of *an* (that): that is, they were not commanded except that they should worship, as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], meaning that He make clear; and ﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 8], meaning that they extinguish.

The majority read *mukhlisin* with a kasra on the *lam*. Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it.

This verse is among the proofs indicating the obligation of intention in acts of worship, because sincerity is an act of the heart. The accusative of *hunafa'* is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *mukhlisin*, so it is of the type of overlapping (*tadakhul*). It is also permissible that it be from the subject of *ya'budu*, and the meaning is: inclining away from all religions towards the religion of Islam.

The people of the language said: The origin of it is that one turns (*yahnif*) towards the religion of Islam, that is, inclines towards it. ﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, that is, perform the prayers at their times and give the zakat at its due time. The prayer and the zakat are singled out because they are among the greatest pillars of the religion.

It has been said: If by the prayer and the zakat is meant what is in the law of the People of the Book of prayer and zakat, then the matter is clear. If what is meant is what is in our law, then the meaning of His commanding them with both in the two scriptures is that He commanded them to follow our law, and both are among what was commanded in them.

﴿And that is the upright religion﴾, that is, that mentioned: worshipping Allah and making it sincere, and establishing the prayer and zakat, ﴿is the upright religion﴾, that is, the religion of the straight community.

al-Zajjaj said: That is the religion of the straight community, so *al-qayyima* is an adjective of an omitted noun.

al-Khalil said: *Al-qayyima* is the plural of *al-qayyim*, and *al-qayyim* means the upright one.

al-Farra' said: He attributed the religion to *al-qayyima*, which is its description, because the two words differ. He also said: It is an attribution of a thing to itself, and the *ha'* (feminine marker) entered for praise and emphasis.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, clarified the condition of the two groups in the Hereafter after clarifying their condition in this world, and said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell﴾. The relative pronoun is the subject of *inna*, *al-mushrikin* is coordinated with it, and its predicate is ﴿in the fire of Hell﴾, and ﴿abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun implied in the predicate. It is also permissible that His saying *wal-mushrikin* be in the genitive case, coordinated with *ahl al-kitab*. The meaning of their being in the fire of Hell is that they will go to it on the Day of Resurrection. The indication in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those previously mentioned among the People of the Book and the polytheists, who are characterised by being in the fire of Hell and abiding in it, ﴿they are the worst of creation﴾, that is, of the creatures. It is said: *bara'a* means "he created," *al-bari'* is the Creator, and *al-bariyya* is the creation.

The majority read *al-bariyya* without a hamza in both places. Nafi' and Ibn Dhakwan read it with a hamza in both places.

al-Farra' said: If you take *al-bariyya* from *al-bara'* (dust), the angels do not enter under this word. If you take it from *bariytu al-qalam* (I shaped the pen, meaning I made it), then they enter.

Some have said that the hamza is the original form, since one says "Allah bara'a al-khalq bi-l-hamz," meaning He originated and invented the creation. From this is His saying: ﴿before We bring it into being﴾ [al-Hadid: 22]. But the hamza was lightened, and its lightening was made obligatory according to the majority of the Arabs.

Then He explained the state of the other group, saying: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, meaning those who combined faith with righteous action, those are the ones described by this: ﴿they are the best of creation﴾. He said: What is meant is that those are the worst of creation in his time (ﷺ), and it is not far-fetched that among the disbelieving nations there may be someone worse than them. And these are the best of creation in his time (ﷺ), and it is not far-fetched that among the believers of earlier nations there may be someone better than them.

﴿Their reward with their Lord﴾, meaning their recompense with their Creator in return for what proceeded from them of faith and righteous action: ﴿Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow﴾. What is meant by "Gardens of Eden" is the middlemost and best of the gardens. It is said: "adana bi-l-makan ya'dunu adnan," meaning he resided. The "ma'din" (source/origin) of a thing is its center and its place of settlement. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And if they are compared to his knowledge, they are compared to a superior one who has settled (qad 'adan)."

We have mentioned in more than one place that if by the gardens are meant the thick-leaved trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is evident; and if what is meant is the totality of the ground's floor and the trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is by reference to its apparent part, which is the trees. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾: they will not leave them nor depart from them, but rather they will remain perpetually in its bliss, continuing in its pleasures. ﴿Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.﴾ The sentence is resumed to explain what Allah has bestowed upon them beyond mere recompense, namely His good pleasure with them, in that they obeyed His command and accepted His laws; and their pleasure with Him, in that they attained of desires what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

It is also permissible that the sentence be a second predicate, or that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause with "qad" understood. ﴿That is for him who fears his Lord﴾: that is, that recompense and good pleasure are for the one in whom the fear of Allah the Exalted arose in this world and who refrained from His disobedience because of that fear which had come to him, not mere fear accompanied by persistent immersion in acts of disobedience to Allah the Exalted, for that is not true fear.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying "munfakkin" (separate), that he said: "barihin" (departing).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you marvel at the rank of the angels with Allah? Recite, if you wish: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'isha, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, who is the most noble of creation before Allah? He said: O 'A'isha, do you not recite ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾?"

Ibn 'Asakir related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) when 'Ali came. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: By Him in whose hand is my soul, this man and his partisans are the victorious on the Day of Resurrection. And the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾. So whenever he came, the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) would say: The best of creation has come."

Ibn 'Adi and Ibn 'Asakir related from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "'Ali is the best of creation."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to 'Ali: It is you and your partisans on the Day of Resurrection, well-pleased and well-pleasing."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the best of creation? They said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah. He said: A man who holds the bridle of his horse in the way of Allah, whenever an alarm sounds he mounts it. Shall I not inform you of the worst of creation? They said: Yes. (p-1645) He said: The one who asks by Allah but does not give by Him."

Ahmad said: Ishaq ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Abu Ma'shar narrated to us, from Abu Wahb, the client of Abu Hurayra, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Aisha, who said: "The surah *Lam yakun* was revealed in Mecca."

Abu Nu'aym transmitted in *al-Ma'rifa* from Isma'il ibn Abi Hakim al-Muzani, who said: Fadl told me: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Allah listens to the recitation of ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾, and says: 'Rejoice, My servant, by My might and My majesty, I will surely grant you in Paradise until you are content.'" Ibn Kathir said: "This is a very strange hadith."

Abu Musa al-Madini transmitted it from Matar al-Muzani, or al-Madani, in similar wording.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: 'Allah has commanded me to recite to you ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾.' He said: 'Did He name me to you?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he wept."

Ahmad, Ibn Qani' in *Mu'jam al-Sahaba*, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hayya al-Badri, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾ to its end, Jibril said: 'O Messenger of Allah, your Lord commands you to recite it to Ubayy.' The Prophet ﷺ said to Ubayy: 'Jibril has commanded me to recite this surah to you.' Ubayy said: 'And was I mentioned there, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he wept."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is said: "I unfastened the thing and it became unfastened," meaning it separated. The meaning is that they were not departing from their disbelief nor ceasing from it, ﴿until there came to them the clear proof﴾. It has also been said that *infikak* means cessation and reaching an end, that is: they would not reach the end of their lifespans and die until there came to them the clear proof. It has also been said that *munfakkin* means "leaving" (ceasing): that is, their term would not end until there came to them the clear proof. It is said: "So-and-so did not cease (*ma infakka*) standing," meaning he did not stop standing. The root of *fakk* is opening, and from it comes *fakk al-khalkhal* (unfastening the anklet).

It has also been said that *munfakkin* means "departing": that is, they would not depart or leave this world until there came to them the clear proof.

Ibn Kaysan said: The meaning is that the People of the Book were not abandoning the description of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent. But when he was sent, they envied him and denied him. This is like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 89]. According to this, His saying "and the polytheists" means that they did not speak ill of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent, for they used to call him "the Trustworthy." But when he was sent, they turned hostile to him and spoke ill of him.

It has been said: *munfakkin* means "perishing," from their saying: "his spine became unfastened," meaning it separated and did not rejoin, so he perished. The meaning is: they were not punished or destroyed except after the proof had been established against them.

It has been said that the polytheists are the People of the Book, so that it is a description of them, because they said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and "Uzayr is the son of Allah."

al-Wahidi said: The meaning of the verse is God Most High informing about the disbelievers that they would not cease from their disbelief and their association of others with Allah until Muhammad ﷺ came to them with the Qur'an, which made clear to them their error and their ignorance, and called them to faith. This is an explanation of the blessing and of being rescued by him from ignorance and error. The verse refers to those from both groups who believed.

He said: This verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in its structure and its exegesis. Great scholars have stumbled over it, and have taken in its interpretation paths that do not lead them to the correct understanding.

The correct view is what I have informed you of. So praise Allah, who has brought you its explanation without ambiguity or difficulty.

He said: That the clear proof is Muhammad ﷺ is shown by the fact that it (the verse) explained it and put it in apposition (*badal*, substitute) to it, saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah reciting purified scriptures﴾, meaning what the scriptures contain of writings in them, which is the Qur'an. This is also shown by the fact that he used to recite from memory, not from a book. End of his words.

It has also been said that the verse is a report of what the People of the Book and the polytheists used to say: that they would not depart from their religion until the promised Prophet was sent. But when he was sent, they split apart, as Allah related about them in this surah.

The clear proof, according to what the majority have said, is Muhammad ﷺ, because he himself is a clear proof and an argument. For this reason Allah named him "a radiant lamp."

Allah, glory be to Him, explained this general "clear proof" by His saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾, so the matter became manifest and it was made clear that he is what is meant by "the clear proof."

Abu Muslim said: What is meant by "the clear proof" is the messengers in general, and the meaning is: until there come to them messengers from Allah, who are the angels, reciting to them purified scriptures. The first view is more preferable.

The majority read ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾. Ibn Mas'ud read: "The polytheists and the People of the Book." Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a reading given in the manner of explanation, not in the manner of recitation.

al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i read *wal-mushrikun* (and the polytheists) with the *raf'* (nominative) case, in coordination with the relative pronoun.

Ubayy read: ﴿So those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not...﴾ (*fa-ma kana*).

The majority read ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾ with *rasulun* in the nominative, as a *badal kull min kull* (a full substitute for the whole, for emphasis), or as a *badal ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion).

al-Zajjaj said: *Rasulun* is in the nominative as a substitute for "the clear proof."

al-Farra' said: It is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject: that is, "it is a messenger" or "he is a messenger."

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *rasulan* in the accusative, as a *qat'* (separation). The phrase *min Allah* is attached to an omitted element which is a description of *rasul*, meaning: "coming from Allah." It is also permissible for it to be attached to *rasul* itself. The meaning is that he recites what the scriptures contain of writings in them, because he ﷺ used to recite from memory, not from a book, as has already been mentioned.

Sahib al-Nazm said: *Kutub* here means a ruling, like His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers shall surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], meaning He ruled. By this is answered what has been said: that *suhuf* are the books, so how could He say ﴿purified scriptures, in them are books﴾?

The exegetes said: The People of the Book were continuously united until Allah sent Muhammad. But when he was sent, they split over his matter and differed. Some of them believed in him and others disbelieved.

He singled out the People of the Book, although others were like them in dividing after the coming of the clear proof, because they were people of knowledge. When they divided, those who had no scripture were included in this description. The exception in His saying ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ is a "restricted" exception from the most general of times: that is, they did not divide at any time except after the clear proof had come to them, namely the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with the glorious law and the white path.

It has been said: "The clear proof" is the explanation that is in their books, that he is a sent prophet, as in His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ except after the knowledge had come to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: From the beginning of the surah to His saying ﴿upright books﴾, its ruling concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who believed.

His saying ﴿And they did not divide...﴾ and so on concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who did not believe after the proofs had been established.

The clause ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause, serving to rebuke and reprimand them for what they did of dividing after the clear proof had come. That is: and the situation is that they were not commanded in their books except for the purpose that they should worship Allah and make Him one, while ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, that is, making their religion pure for Him, glory be to Him, or making themselves pure for Him in religion. It has been said that the *lam* in *liya'budu* (that they might worship) has the meaning of *an* (that): that is, they were not commanded except that they should worship, as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], meaning that He make clear; and ﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 8], meaning that they extinguish.

The majority read *mukhlisin* with a kasra on the *lam*. Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it.

This verse is among the proofs indicating the obligation of intention in acts of worship, because sincerity is an act of the heart. The accusative of *hunafa'* is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *mukhlisin*, so it is of the type of overlapping (*tadakhul*). It is also permissible that it be from the subject of *ya'budu*, and the meaning is: inclining away from all religions towards the religion of Islam.

The people of the language said: The origin of it is that one turns (*yahnif*) towards the religion of Islam, that is, inclines towards it. ﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, that is, perform the prayers at their times and give the zakat at its due time. It has been said: If by the prayer and the zakat is meant what is in the law of the People of the Book of prayer and zakat, then the matter is clear. The meaning of their being in the fire of Hell is that they will go to it on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kaysan said: The meaning is that the People of the Book were not abandoning the description of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent. But when he was sent, they envied him and denied him. This is like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 89]. According to this, His saying "and the polytheists" means that they did not speak ill of Muhammad ﷺ until he was sent, for they used to call him "the Trustworthy." But when he was sent, they turned hostile to him and spoke ill of him.

It has been said: *munfakkin* means "perishing," from their saying: "his spine became unfastened," meaning it separated and did not rejoin, so he perished. The meaning is: they were not punished or destroyed except after the proof had been established against them.

It has been said that the polytheists are the People of the Book, so that it is a description of them, because they said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and "Uzayr is the son of Allah."

al-Wahidi said: The meaning of the verse is God Most High informing about the disbelievers that they would not cease from their disbelief and their association of others with Allah until Muhammad ﷺ came to them with the Qur'an, which made clear to them their error and their ignorance, and called them to faith. This is an explanation of the blessing and of being rescued by him from ignorance and error. The verse refers to those from both groups who believed.

He said: This verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in its structure and its exegesis. Great scholars have stumbled over it, and have taken in its interpretation paths that do not lead them to the correct understanding.

The correct view is what I have informed you of. So praise Allah, who has brought you its explanation without ambiguity or difficulty.

He said: That the clear proof is Muhammad ﷺ is shown by the fact that it (the verse) explained it and put it in apposition (*badal*, substitute) to it, saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah reciting purified scriptures﴾, meaning what the scriptures contain of writings in them, which is the Qur'an. This is also shown by the fact that he used to recite from memory, not from a book. End of his words.

It has also been said that the verse is a report of what the People of the Book and the polytheists used to say: that they would not depart from their religion until the promised Prophet was sent. But when he was sent, they split apart, as Allah related about them in this surah.

The clear proof, according to what the majority have said, is Muhammad ﷺ, because he himself is a clear proof and an argument. For this reason Allah named him "a radiant lamp."

Allah, glory be to Him, explained this general "clear proof" by His saying: ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾, so the matter became manifest and it was made clear that he is what is meant by "the clear proof."

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: The clear proof is the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]. Abu Muslim said: What is meant by "the clear proof" is the messengers in general, and the meaning is: until there come to them messengers from Allah, who are the angels, reciting to them purified scriptures. The first view is more preferable.

The majority read ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾. Ibn Mas'ud read: "The polytheists and the People of the Book." Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a reading given in the manner of explanation, not in the manner of recitation.

al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i read *wal-mushrikun* (and the polytheists) with the *raf'* (nominative) case, in coordination with the relative pronoun.

Ubayy read: ﴿So those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not...﴾ (*fa-ma kana*).

The majority read ﴿a messenger from Allah﴾ with *rasulun* in the nominative, as a *badal kull min kull* (a full substitute for the whole, for emphasis), or as a *badal ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion).

al-Zajjaj said: *Rasulun* is in the nominative as a substitute for "the clear proof."

al-Farra' said: It is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject: that is, "it is a messenger" or "he is a messenger."

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *rasulan* in the accusative, as a *qat'* (separation). The phrase *min Allah* is attached to an omitted element which is a description of *rasul*, meaning: "coming from Allah." It is also permissible for it to be attached to *rasul* itself. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *suhuf* (scriptures), with the implied meaning: "reciting purified scriptures sent down from Allah." His saying ﴿reciting purified scriptures﴾ may be another description of *rasul*, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the preceding prepositional phrase.

The meaning of *yatlu* is "recites." It is said: "talā yatlū tilāwa." *Suhuf* is the plural of *sahifa*, which is the container of what is written. The meaning of *muṭahhara* (purified) is that they are free of falsehood and error.

Qatada said: "Purified" means free of falsehood. It has been said: "purified" means free of lies, doubts, and disbelief. The meaning is one. The meaning is that he recites what the scriptures contain of writings in them, because he ﷺ used to recite from memory, not from a book, as has already been mentioned.

His saying ﴿in them are upright books﴾ is a description of *suhuf*, or a circumstantial clause from its pronoun. What is meant is the verses and the rulings written in them. *Qayyima* means straight, upright, correct, firm, from the Arab saying: "the thing stood" when it became straight and sound.

Sahib al-Nazm said: *Kutub* here means a ruling, like His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers shall surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], meaning He ruled. And the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the story of the labourer: "I will surely judge between you two by the Book of Allah," and then he ruled for stoning, though stoning is not in the Book of Allah. So the meaning is: "I will surely judge between you two by the ruling of Allah." By this is answered what has been said: that *suhuf* are the books, so how could He say ﴿purified scriptures, in them are books﴾?

al-Hasan said: By the purified scriptures is meant those that are in heaven, that is, in the Preserved Tablet, as in His saying: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21–22].

﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear proof had come to them.﴾ This sentence is a new independent sentence, to rebuke and reprimand the People of the Book, and to explain that what is attributed to them of not departing was not due to confusion of the matter, but was after the truth had become clear and the right course had become manifest.

The exegetes said: The People of the Book were continuously united until Allah sent Muhammad. But when he was sent, they split over his matter and differed. Some of them believed in him and others disbelieved.

He singled out the People of the Book, although others were like them in dividing after the coming of the clear proof, because they were people of knowledge. When they divided, those who had no scripture were included in this description. The exception in His saying ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ is a "restricted" exception from the most general of times: that is, they did not divide at any time except after the clear proof had come to them, namely the sending of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with the glorious law and the white path.

It has been said: "The clear proof" is the explanation that is in their books, that he is a sent prophet, as in His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ except after the knowledge had come to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: From the beginning of the surah to His saying ﴿upright books﴾, its ruling concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who believed.

His saying ﴿And they did not divide...﴾ and so on concerns those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who did not believe after the proofs had been established.

The clause ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause, serving to rebuke and reprimand them for what they did of dividing after the clear proof had come. That is: and the situation is that they were not commanded in their books except for the purpose that they should worship Allah and make Him one, while ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, that is, making their religion pure for Him, glory be to Him, or making themselves pure for Him in religion. It has been said that the *lam* in *liya'budu* (that they might worship) has the meaning of *an* (that): that is, they were not commanded except that they should worship, as in His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], meaning that He make clear; and ﴿They desire to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 8], meaning that they extinguish.

The majority read *mukhlisin* with a kasra on the *lam*. Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on it.

This verse is among the proofs indicating the obligation of intention in acts of worship, because sincerity is an act of the heart. The accusative of *hunafa'* is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *mukhlisin*, so it is of the type of overlapping (*tadakhul*). It is also permissible that it be from the subject of *ya'budu*, and the meaning is: inclining away from all religions towards the religion of Islam.

The people of the language said: The origin of it is that one turns (*yahnif*) towards the religion of Islam, that is, inclines towards it. ﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, that is, perform the prayers at their times and give the zakat at its due time. The prayer and the zakat are singled out because they are among the greatest pillars of the religion.

It has been said: If by the prayer and the zakat is meant what is in the law of the People of the Book of prayer and zakat, then the matter is clear. If what is meant is what is in our law, then the meaning of His commanding them with both in the two scriptures is that He commanded them to follow our law, and both are among what was commanded in them.

﴿And that is the upright religion﴾, that is, that mentioned: worshipping Allah and making it sincere, and establishing the prayer and zakat, ﴿is the upright religion﴾, that is, the religion of the straight community.

al-Zajjaj said: That is the religion of the straight community, so *al-qayyima* is an adjective of an omitted noun.

al-Khalil said: *Al-qayyima* is the plural of *al-qayyim*, and *al-qayyim* means the upright one.

al-Farra' said: He attributed the religion to *al-qayyima*, which is its description, because the two words differ. He also said: It is an attribution of a thing to itself, and the *ha'* (feminine marker) entered for praise and emphasis.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, clarified the condition of the two groups in the Hereafter after clarifying their condition in this world, and said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell﴾. The relative pronoun is the subject of *inna*, *al-mushrikin* is coordinated with it, and its predicate is ﴿in the fire of Hell﴾, and ﴿abiding therein﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun implied in the predicate. It is also permissible that His saying *wal-mushrikin* be in the genitive case, coordinated with *ahl al-kitab*. The meaning of their being in the fire of Hell is that they will go to it on the Day of Resurrection. The indication in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those previously mentioned among the People of the Book and the polytheists, who are characterised by being in the fire of Hell and abiding in it, ﴿they are the worst of creation﴾, that is, of the creatures. It is said: *bara'a* means "he created," *al-bari'* is the Creator, and *al-bariyya* is the creation.

The majority read *al-bariyya* without a hamza in both places. Nafi' and Ibn Dhakwan read it with a hamza in both places.

al-Farra' said: If you take *al-bariyya* from *al-bara'* (dust), the angels do not enter under this word. If you take it from *bariytu al-qalam* (I shaped the pen, meaning I made it), then they enter.

Some have said that the hamza is the original form, since one says "Allah bara'a al-khalq bi-l-hamz," meaning He originated and invented the creation. From this is His saying: ﴿before We bring it into being﴾ [al-Hadid: 22]. But the hamza was lightened, and its lightening was made obligatory according to the majority of the Arabs.

Then He explained the state of the other group, saying: Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, meaning those who combined faith with righteous action, those are the ones described by this: ﴿they are the best of creation﴾. He said: What is meant is that those are the worst of creation in his time (ﷺ), and it is not far-fetched that among the disbelieving nations there may be someone worse than them. And these are the best of creation in his time (ﷺ), and it is not far-fetched that among the believers of earlier nations there may be someone better than them.

﴿Their reward with their Lord﴾, meaning their recompense with their Creator in return for what proceeded from them of faith and righteous action: ﴿Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow﴾. What is meant by "Gardens of Eden" is the middlemost and best of the gardens. It is said: "adana bi-l-makan ya'dunu adnan," meaning he resided. The "ma'din" (source/origin) of a thing is its center and its place of settlement. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And if they are compared to his knowledge, they are compared to a superior one who has settled (qad 'adan)."

We have mentioned in more than one place that if by the gardens are meant the thick-leaved trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is evident; and if what is meant is the totality of the ground's floor and the trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is by reference to its apparent part, which is the trees. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾: they will not leave them nor depart from them, but rather they will remain perpetually in its bliss, continuing in its pleasures. ﴿Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.﴾ The sentence is resumed to explain what Allah has bestowed upon them beyond mere recompense, namely His good pleasure with them, in that they obeyed His command and accepted His laws; and their pleasure with Him, in that they attained of desires what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

It is also permissible that the sentence be a second predicate, or that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause with "qad" understood. ﴿That is for him who fears his Lord﴾: that is, that recompense and good pleasure are for the one in whom the fear of Allah the Exalted arose in this world and who refrained from His disobedience because of that fear which had come to him, not mere fear accompanied by persistent immersion in acts of disobedience to Allah the Exalted, for that is not true fear.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying "munfakkin" (separate), that he said: "barihin" (departing).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you marvel at the rank of the angels with Allah? By Him in whose hand is my soul, the rank of the believing servant with Allah on the Day of Resurrection is greater than the rank of an angel. Recite, if you wish: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'isha, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, who is the most noble of creation before Allah? He said: O 'A'isha, do you not recite ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾?"

Ibn 'Asakir related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) when 'Ali came. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: By Him in whose hand is my soul, this man and his partisans are the victorious on the Day of Resurrection. And the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾. So whenever he came, the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) would say: The best of creation has come."

Ibn 'Adi and Ibn 'Asakir related from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "'Ali is the best of creation."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the best of creation﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to 'Ali: It is you and your partisans on the Day of Resurrection, well-pleased and well-pleasing."

Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ali, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ahmad related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the best of creation? They said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah. He said: A man who holds the bridle of his horse in the way of Allah, whenever an alarm sounds he mounts it. Shall I not inform you of the worst of creation? They said: Yes. (p-1645) He said: The one who asks by Allah but does not give by Him."

Ahmad said: Ishaq ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Abu Ma'shar narrated to us, from Abu Wahb, the client of Abu Hurayra, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.
